Mr. ADSHElAD: I hope I am in order under this item. The last time the question of the Calgary post office came up, the Chairman allowed the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to discuss the matter at some length and the Minister of Public Works to reply. When I endeavoured to follow them I was informed that I was out of order and that I must discuss the matter in connection with the Alberta estimates. I wish, not to make a special plea, but to direct the attention of the Minister of Public Works and the committee to the fact that the government are losing money by the way in which they are handling post office affairs in Calgary. A retrospect of what has happened in that city might very well go on Hansard.
In 1911 the city of Calgary had a three-storey stone building which was a post office and which was occupied also by the Dominion Lands office. My hon. friends to my right at that time got into power and with all good intentions they pulled down the postoffice in order to build a larger one because the accommodation there was not adequate. They also bought lots to the east of that site for $3'12,46o, with the intention of erecting a building such as the Minister of Public Works has just described for Saskatoon. The war came on and they put a board fence around those vacant lots and for fifteen years the people of Calgary have had to look at that board fence right in the heart of the city where my hon. friends pulled down these buildings for the purpose of erecting a new one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Where are the stones
now?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not know. I inquired about that last year and I could not get any information in regard to the matter. If I could make a comparison I would say; Look at the square west of the Ottawa post office which is just being modelled into a
park, and I would ask the committee ta visualize if they can a square of that size in the heart of the city of Ottawa surrounded by a board fence, and the people of Ottawa being allowed to look at that for fifteen years and to go without a post office altogether. Comparisons, they say, are odious to the general public. I may say to the Minister of Public Works that the city of Calgary is more important than the city of Ottawa. I do not mean it is more important politically but it is more important financially. I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that of all the cities in the Dominion, Calgary stands fifth in regard to bank clearings. The bank clearings for Ottawa for April, 1928, were $33,727,739. For Oalgary for the same month the bank clearings amounted to $50,656,715. In other words, although we are the fifth city of the Dominion in regard to bank clearings for the month of April, we have no post office but we have to look at that blank square across a hideous board fence. In the matter of post office revenue for the year ended the 31st March, 1927, the collections at Calgary amounted to $566,871, that city being the seventh in the Dominion of Canada. It was ahead of Quebec, Moncton, Edmonton and most of the other cities, and still we have no post office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How did it stand with
regard to the city of Ottawa?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It was within a few
thousand dollars of the post office revenues of the city of Ottawa. I propose to deal with the rentals that we are paying in Calgary and to show that we are losing money by the process that is going on. I asked for information as to the annual rental of the post office building which we have in Calgary and the answer I received from the Minister of Public Works was that we are paying a rental of 70,000 per annum for a gross space of a little over 70,000 square feet. I think the minister the other day observed in the house that as regards some building which was proposed for the Bureau of Statistics the rental asked was a dollar per square foot, and he thought that altogether too high for a building of that sort-

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The best we could do
was $1.25.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
-so he decided to purchase a building. In Calgary we have been paying under lease nearly $1 per square foot, a figure which I consider too high for the rental of that particular building. If we were to capitalize that $70,000, not of course including depreciation or maintenance, at five

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
per cent we could erect a building at a value of $1,400,000 and at four per cent we could erect a building at a value of $1,750,000. The minister has just told us that in some city, I think it was Saskatoon, they propose to erect, on a lot somewhat similar in length and size to the lot I have indicated we have in Calgary, a five-story building, for the sum of $600,000. If a building of that size can be constructed for $600,000, the interest and depreciation on it would not nearly reach the $70,000 of rent which we are paying for our post office and the Dominion land office in Calgary. I suppose the matter could be arranged under the plan of a sinking fund. I know the minister has not inserted an item for it in the estimates this year, but there is a phase of the situation to which I wish to draw his attention and that is that the lease on the building which they have rented for $70,000 a year expires at the end of 1929. I would suggest to the minister that if he wants to save money; if he wants to be economical; if he desires to have in Calgary a building which will belong to the Dominion and which in interest, depreciation and maintenance will not cost more than $70,000 a year, he should make some plan or have some prospect of erecting a building there whereby the government will have a building of their own prior to the expiration of the lease. I think preparations should be made at once with the idea of providing a building. I hope the government has no idea of purchasing the building in which the post office is now located. It would be very much against the wishes of the people of the city of Calgary if you purchased that building and left vacant the lots upon which the post office was originally built, together with the $312,465 worth of lots which were purchased for the express purpose of erecting a building right next to the old post office building site. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to this question from a business standpoint, and not simply give me the usual platitude, "I am going to give the matter serious consideration." It should be considered from a business standpoint, and also from another standpoint. The government did intend before the war to build a public building in Calgary, and for the last fifteen years not only has that hideous board fence been left in the heart of the city, but property values all around have depreciated, and what is more, the government is actually losing money by continuing the present conditions. You have no building of your own, and it is costing more for rentals than the interest and depreciation 
on the new buildings would amount to. I would ask the minister what he proposes to do when the lease on this building expires in 1929. Does he propose to renew the lease for three or five years, or what preparations are being made for putting the thing on a business basis and relieving the people of Calgary from that hideous eyesore in the very heart of the city?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I will answer my hon.
friend as far as I can. I think he will realize that it is quite impossible for me to say at the moment what we can do on the expiration of a lease which does not expire until some time in 1929.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Some preparation is
necessary before the lease actually expires if you are going to put up a building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am bound to tell my
hon. friend that even if we had come to a decision, we might not think it was in the public interest to say just what that decision was this far ahead of time. But I will be very frank in stating that we have come to no decision in regard to renewing the lea^e.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
And no decision as to
buying the present building?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is in the same category. There are a number of buildings in the smaller places throughout the country, old bank buildings occasionally, and other buildings that have been purchased in the past for the public services and turned into a public building, and among the applications that we have before us at the present time are a few asking us to purchase buildings already in existence, which no doubt could be purchased very much cheaper than we could construct a new building. That proposition was made to us in the city of Saskatoon. There was a building there that we were asked to purchase, and no doubt we could have purchased it and got floor space much cheaper than we could consrtuet a new building. The same is true of many other places, but of course these buildings would never look very much like a post office, and there is just the difficulty. If it is in a town where you consider that you are getting exceptionally good value, and where possibly you would not construct a new building costing from $20,000 to $30,000, my view would be that we might be justified in buying a building in some of these places if the people were satisfied with the accom-

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
modation it would provide, say a building costing 810,000 or $12,000, perhaps half the cost of constructing a new building. So far as Calgary is concerned, there is certainly no decision in favour of buying a building for customs and post office and government services generally.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is a customs office there already.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understand that. I want to say further, as regards the prices my hon. friend mentions-and prices were also mentioned in connection with Saskatoon-that they are altogether out of proportion to the figures shown in the actual tenders. So far as Calgary is concerned, tenders were called for in 1914 for the construction of a building which was considered sufficient to meet the requirements of Calgary at that time, and the lowest tender received was for $1,399,000, and the highest tender, $1,703,000. There were five tenders altogether. There is no question that the cost of the building has increased enormously since that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Surely the minister has
no idea of purchasing the building in which the post office is now located. I asked that question last year, and Hansard will show that the minister said that they did not have that intention. I hope there is no doubt about that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will be very frank in saying to my hon. friend that there is absolutely no change in the condition from what it was a year ago, and no serious consideration has been given in the last year to purchasing that building. That answer was true then, and it is true now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If there was any such
intention, it would raise a terrible disturbance among the people of Calgary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would ask the committee
to look at page 32 of the estimates and compare the amounts being voted for the three western provinces, and ask hon. members if in their opinion Alberta has been fairly dealt with. In 1927-28 Manitoba was voted $114,000; Saskatchewan, $212,950; and Alberta, $32,000. In 1928-29 Manitoba is being voted $105,700; Saskatchewan, $353,850; and Alberta, $56,850.
I also see in looking over the estimates that no provision is made for a public building in Camrose, for which there was an appropriation in the estimates in 1926, and
which was brought before the house last session. I would ask the Minister of Public Works if he can give any reason why that vote, which was considered and approved by the government and placed in the estimates, has been withdrawn.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: That ought to be easy to explain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I gave my hon. friend
the answer last year, and there is nothing I can add to what I then said. Camrose is in this long list of applications that we have here, where the need has not been considerec as urgent as in the other places for which provision is being made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister says it does
not appear to have been considered as urgent as the need in other places. I will ask the committee to follow these figures I am going to give in regard to votes passed this session for public buildings at different places. For the province of Quebec there are two votes: St. Jacques, population 1,714, revenue $2,017; Waterloo, population 2,000, revenue $6,356; Durham, Ontario, population 1,640, revenue $5,060; Rockland, Ontario, population 3,156, revenue $2,412; Rosthern, Sask., population 1,500, revenue $6,248; Tisdale, Sask , population 900, revenue $6,957. Now I come to the town of Camrose, in the province of Alberta, which has a population of 2,000 and a revenue of $13,186-more than double the amount of the revenue of the other post offices for which votes have been passed this session. In addition there is a sub customs office there with a revenue of over $50,000 a year. In view of these facts I think the minister should state to the house what is the policy of the government in determining whether or not a town is entitled to a post office.
In case the minister may think that I am prejudiced in putting forward the claims of Camrose, let me read an article from the Camrose Canadian of January 5, 1928. It is a Liberal paper published in Camrose, and I feel sure the minister will accept this article as fairly representing the facts. It is headed, Why the Delay?
Away back in 1911 the Department of Public Works in the Dominion government purchased a very desirable site in Camrose for the erection of a post office building. The volume of business transacted at the local post office at that time warranted this action on the part of the government, and it was the hope of the citizens of the town, and residents of the surrounding country, that a building in keeping with the needs of the community would be ready for use within a reasonable time.

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
With the completion of the various railroads, radiating in all directions from Camrose, resulting in the creation of many new villages and country post offices, the local office acted as a gathering and distributing centre for a large proportion of the mail in and out of this portion of the province. This meant a tremendous increase in the amount of mail passing through the Camrose office. The selection of Camrose as the location of the normal school for northern Alberta, the building of the Camrose Lutheran college, and the establishment of several large wholesale houses, made it necessary to provide more commodious and up-to-date quarters for the proper handling of the rapidly growing business of the post office.
Sixteen years have passed since the site was purchased, and the lots lie as they did in 1911, bare a3 the virgin prairie. No use whatever has been made of them. Eight thousand dollars of the peoples' money have been tied up in this unproductive investment all those years. The town treasury has been deprived of a sum of money amounting to approximately $4,000 which, had the property remained in private hands, would have been paid to the town as taxes. In the interval the needs of Camrose for larger post office accommodation has been growing from year to year.
I wish the minister to note particularly this part:
It is not necessary to draw the attention of the public to the utterly inadequate premises in which the business is carried on at the present time. The unsatisfactory conditions are familiar to all. The space in the building for the public, as well as the employees, is far too limited. Frequently it is impossible to enter the building, particularly at the noon hour, when the schools close and the students call for mail. It is clearly obvious that the clerks are cramped for space, especially when scores of mail hags are dumped into the rear part of the building. As a result of overcrowding, the air becomes so foul that it is sickening, and the wonder is that the employees whose work compels them to remain in the unhealthy atmosphere for hours at a time, have so far escaped serious illness. Under such unfavourable conditions in any other place of business it is doubtful if the public would be given the same courteous service which is invariably rendered by the clerks of the Camrose office. In all probability the health officer would interfere and insist on better sanitary conditions.
It was a Liberal government that purchased the property for the proposed building. That government was defeated later in the year. Efforts were made to interest the newly-formed Conservative government to carry out the program begun by its predecessors, but without avail. Then came the Great War when all public works in Canada were suspended. Following the defeat of the Union government, with the Liberals again in power, hopes were revived that it, which recognized the needs of the community in 1911, would feel its responsibility and carry out the undertaking.
In the preliminary estimates presented to parliament last session, an item was included for the construction of the Camrose public building. As a result, high hopes prevailed in the hearts of the people of Camrose that the long delayed building would shortly become an established fact. But such was not to be; something miscarried. What happened has 
remained a mystery to the present time. When the iten) was up for discussion little, if any, support was offered in its favour from the government side of the house. Strange as it may seem the cause of the constituency was championed by opposition members. The final outcome of the matter was its entire withdrawal from the estimates. The same government which placed it there allowed it to perish unsupported. No reason whatever was given for their indifferent action. Surely we are entitled to an explanation. Sinister motives on the part of the government were imputed for the unusual treatment.
The Canadian does not care to view the matter in that light, rather it believes that some of the fault rested with us. During the debate on the item it was very clear that little was known of our requirements, some members even being ignorant of the existence of such a place as Camrose. Our case had not been presented in a manner which would demonstrate the importance of the situation. We believe our claim is fair and just, and can be supported by the facts, and the government should be made aware of these facts at the earliest possible moment.
Some very interesting figures are revealed by the census taken during the summer of 1926. That extensive, fertile territory, through which the Battle river flows, extending from Wetas-kiwin on the w-est to Hardisty, and from Yegre-ville on the north to Stettler, is shown to have a population greater than any other rural area of like size in Alberta. Being nearly one hundred miles square, it combines an area equal to that portion of western Ontario lying south of a line drawn from Toronto to Sarnia. In this block of highly improved parkland country, there is a population of 50,000 people, over 8,000 occupied farms, and 50 towns and villages.
Many of the urban centres are shown to have populations ranging from 200 to 500, and Camrose, located fairly near the centre of this territory, had a population of over 2,000 in June 1926. More than twenty banks serve the needs of this thriving region, and the same number of coal mines are in operation most of the year. Much of this country has been settled for over twenty-five years, and in that period many millions of dollars' worth of farm products have gone to swell the export trade of the Dominion. The wheat grown in this territory in 1927 exceeded 25 million bushels, and the value of all the products of the farms and mines during the past year will approximate at least $40,000,000.
Now for what really hurts. Never has one dollar of federal money been expended in this large and important part of western Canada for public buildings of any kind. Does that seem fair? We doubt if any other section of Canada of like size and importance has received such treatment. How much longer must we wait?
It will be noted, Mr. Chairman, that the article says that the needs of Camrose have never been fairly presented to parliament. When I came down here in 1922 as the representative of what was then the constituency of Victoria and in which Camrose was included, it is a well-known fact that the policy of the government at that time was not to spend any money on public buildings as we

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
were still feeling the effects of the heavy war expenditure. Therefore I made no representations in regard to this post office. But within the last few years the present government has changed that policy, and I certainly made such representations that in 1926 an amount was placed in the estimates to provide for this building. Having secured that recognition, I felt I had gone far enough to convince the government that we were entitled to the post office building. When the item came up for discussion last session there was no opposition offered to it, and therefore I did not deem it necessary to take up the time of the house by giving any further explanation. But now that that estimate has been withdrawn, I desire to endorse everything that is contained in this leading article which I have just quoted, and to point out to the committee that Camrose is one the most flourishing towns in western Canada. It is a very important railroad centre, lines radiating in eight different directions; there are three wholesale houses; a large normal school for the northern half of Alberta is located there, and a large Lutheran college. The result is that when all these people attempt to get in, especially when schools and colleges are out, and the vrfiole-sale houses are closed, the present accommodation in the post office is entirely inadequate. I feel sure that the government does not want to treat Camrose unfairly, and I would ask the minister to give some promise that in the supplementary estimates an item will be provided in this connection.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know something of the
needs of Camrose. I know the town, and 1 do not agree with my hon. friend that the need there is more urgent than in many other places on our list. I do not think it is as urgent as any of those that have been granted. It is on the list that we have under consideration and it will receive the best consideration we can give it. But I think my hon. friend heard me say that it would be quite impossible for me to pi'omise him or anyone else that it will be put in the estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: On what basis did the government consider it urgent in 1926 to put a vote in the estimates if it is not urgent now? Was it more urgent then than it is to-day? What has occurred to cause the government to change their opinion?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I was not in charge of the department when the vote was included in 1926. I go over the information we have and submit to the treasury board first of all, and afterwards to council, a certain list of appropriations. It did not seem to either the treasury board or council, nor did it appear to me, that this was as urgent as some of the other places whose applications were granted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does the minister think that the previous minister made a mistake in including the item in 1926?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are certain times
when it looks as if a town is growing very rapidly. We have a great many towns that are growing rapidly and the accommodation of several years ago is not adequate to-day. It might have appeared in 1926 that the town was going ahead very fast and additional facilities would have to be provided; but perhaps when the next record comes in-returns for the following year-the increase does not look nearly so marked. When all these circumstances are considered we have to make the best recommendation we can.
At six o'clo'ck the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Alberta-Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $17,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Just before six o'clock I understood the minister to say that some places for which we have voted money for public buildings showed evidence of increased growth of one kind or another. Would the minister tell us more about that in regard to some of the places for which we have already voted money?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: The item last under discussion, the public building for Saskatoon, is an outstanding example.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Would the minister leave out the cities and take up some of the rural places which I mentioned this afternon?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: There are very few buildings in the whole vote. To what does my hon. friend refer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I gave a list this afternoon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend expects me to go over all the places for which we have voted money, although there are not many of them. Will my hon. friend name any particular place and ask to have a comparison made?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not wish the minister to go over all the places, but I gave a list of six this afternoon, two in Quebec, two in Ontario and two in Saskatchewan, small rural
Supply-Public Works-Alberta

towns similar to Camrose. I understood the argument of the minister to be that some of these places were starting to grow and were therefore entitled to money for a public building, but I contend that Camrose has shown as much growth as any of them, if not more. For instance, take Rosthern, Saskatchewan; the postal revenues in 1924 amounted to $6,429, while in 1927 they totalled $6,248. Then there is Durham, Ontario; in 1924 the postal revenue amounted to $7,145, and in 1927 it was $5,683. Take Waterloo, Quebec; in 1924 the postal revenue was $6,673 and in 1927 it amounted to $5,731. Personally I cannot see any evidence in these cases of the growth to which the minister referred.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: All the circumstances,, the accommodation which is being used, the opportunity for obtaining 'better accommodation and the urgency for making a change of some kind, are looked into, and the department arrives at the best conclusion possible under the circumstances.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have heard the Prime Minister say time and again in this house that the government are but a committee of the house, responsible to the house for all their actions, and further that the government are responsible for carrying out the wishes of this house. In the supplementary estimates of 1926 there appeared an item for the construction of this building at C'amrose. The committee will remember that the supplementary estimates and in fact many of the main estiates were not passed in the first session of 1926. On December 9 of that year this house was called together primarily for the purpose of passing the estimates so that the government would not have to issue governor general's warrants; I remember that the supplementary estimates at that session contained this item for the Camrose post office, which item was passed by this house. That means that this house instructed the government to construct this building at Camrose. When the main estimates came up the next year, because of the fact that the building could not be proceeded with immediately after the item was passed the estimates did not contain any item for the Camrose post office. What I want to know is this: Is the Prime Minister satisfied in his own mind that the government are a committee of this house and as such are willing to carry out the instructions of this house? If so, will the minister explain why, after this house once passed this particular item, the government so far forgot their duty to the house that they did not proceed with this work? I think that should be explained before we go any further.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: The hon. member heard my explanation a year ago and he has heard what has been said so far this session; the department have gone over all the available data and have come to the best conclusion possible as to what shall be recommended to the treasury board and to council. That is all I can say; I cannot add anything to that statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then do I take it from what the minister says that he does not believe in the principle enunciated by the Prime Minister, that the government are but a committee of this house and responsible to the house? Does the minister wish to repudiate that statement by the Prime Minister?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister is evidently doing it under the circumstances.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister say there was any evidence came up to show that Camrose was not just as much entitled to a post office this year as in 1926, when this estimate was first passed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will certainly say there was no evidence to lead the department, the treasury board or council to believe that Camrose was more entitled to a building than a great many other places whose applications were being refused at that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: That was not the question I asked. Evidently this matter was considered by the government and the treasury board in 1926 when the item was placed in the estimates, and I am asking the minister now if any new evidence came up which would justify the government or the treasury board in cutting this item out of the estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite wrong when he says the item was cut out of the estimates; that was not done. It was in estimates which lapsed, and another set of estimates was made up. For reasons which the government considered sufficient from all available data, the item was not inserted again. That is all I can say to my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would just like to say
to the hon. minister that the town of Camrose has been making rapid growth. Only this last year a large business block costing over $40,000 has been erected there. A very large hotel, estimated to cost $90,000, has just been completed, and also several new churches,

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
all costing very large sums of money. All the evidence is to the effect that the town of Camrose is prospering and growing rapidly, and therefore it seems rather difficult to understand why the government consider this matter in 1926-because I feel sure that it would not have gone in the estimates unless they had considered it-and later cut it out. As far as the evidence of development is concerned, the government cannot produce anything to show that the town of Camrose is going back. I should like to know for what other reason the government decided to leave this item out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will the minister ask his deputy to give him the reasons for putting the item in the 1926 supplementary estimates, and his reasons for leaving it out in the 1927 main estimates? There must have been good and sufficient reason why it was put in in 1926, and no doubt there were good and sufficient reasons why it was 'taken out in 1927. Would he let us have the information with regard to those two particular items of procedure?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should like to
ask the minister regarding this installation of pick-up table.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is a patented device, known as the Cummins pick-up. It is thought to be the best device available for picking up the letters from the floor, or the table, or whatever place they are on at the particular time. I have never used one of these machines myself, but they are a distinct type, and very well known. I believe that it is the type of machine that investigation has shown to meet the requirements, and is the best machine available at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Where is it manufactured?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think it is an American concern; the Interprovincial Equipment Company, Queen street, Ottawa, is the Canadian representative. I have a note to that effect, so I take it that it is an American concern.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it being installed in all the large offices?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think the investigations that were made with regard to the new terminal station at Montreal were made in New York and various other places. If my memory serves me right, their information was that this was the type found most satisfactory there. It is what the post office asks for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I asked the minister
two questions, and I hope he will be given time to answer them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is this pick-up table supposed to be a labour-saving device, and if so, is there any actual saving in connection with it? Will it save any extra help and cut down the overhead, or is it a laboursaving device which will allow men to stand around and do nothing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I will give my hon. friend all the information I have on the subject. By authority of an order in council passed on July 15. 1927, 10 Cummins pick-up tables were purchased at a cost of $3,500 each, from the Interprovincial Equipment Company, of Ottawa, four of the tables being for Montreal and six for Toronto. This equipment is a patented article, made in Chicago, and is the only mechanical pick-up table on the market. For this reason there was no object in calling for public tenders, and a contract was entered into without this being done. This is the information which I was unable to give to my hon. friend a few minutes ago. At the time these tables were purchased the following memorandum was submitted by the Deputy Postmaster General on May 16, 1927, regarding the advantages of the same:
This machine has been under consideration by the department for some time, as a means of economy, and for the expediting and prompt despatch of letter mail. This type is the only mechanical pickup table and stacker produced commercially, either in this country or the United States.
Other experimental types were investigated, and as there were no plans available, sketches were made for the purpose of a general report to this department at the time. The Mayer type, of which only one was constructed for test purposes in the New York post office, was too cumbersome and complicated, as will be seen on reference to the sketch mentioned. The output of the Rotary type developed by the United States government for smaller offices has been disappointing and unfavourably reported on by the majority of United States postmasters who have used them.
The Cummins type has produced the most favourable comment, and it has the advantage of having passed through the experimental stage, and being a standard article substantially built and produced by a reliable firm.
The stacker attachment alone will do the work now performed by a porter, and the statement made by the concern introducing this machine "that it will save its own cost in a year" is well founded, as the labour charge during the peak load period can be reduced 50 per cent in the "facing up" process.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No one is denying that
this is a labour saving device, but are we going to save anything by using it?

Supply-Public Works-Alberta

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: They say that the tea that were purchased will pay for themselves in a year, by the saving in labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT

friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister answer the questions I put to him a few moments ago?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am sorry, but I will have to ask my hon. friend to repeat them.

speechtext:
In the supplementary
estimates for 1926 there was an item for a post office at Camrose. I would like to ask the minister the reason for including that item in the estimates. What representations were made that finally led to this item being in the supplementary estimates of 1926? I will put one question at a time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I must apologize to my
hon. friend for not having answered that before. He added to that the request that I would ask my deputy just how that had been done. He would not have added that to his question had he realized just what I propose to tell him about the procedure. The deputy is not in the council when these matters are being considered and the decisions really made. Perhaps that will be a sufficient answer as regards the deputy.
Of course as my hon. friend knows I was not in the department at the time. My predecessor, after considering the question, decided to place this item in the supplementary estimates. The procedure is this. I will in a few days put before the treasury board a large number of items for the supplementary estimates. I am not sure yet what fraction of them I will get. They first go before the treasury board and the treasury board in their discretion say:	Well, we will cut this

out and we will leave that in. Sometimes, but not often, something that is cut out by the treasury board is replaced by the cabinet council when the estimates are subsequently submitted to them. It is quite impossible, as my hon. friend will understand, for me to tell him the particular history of this one item out of very many that went through at a time when I was not in charge of the department. I know it was in the supplementaries and I know it did not come through the treasury board and council at the time that the next estimates appeared. That is all I can say in regard to the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT

Has the minister any

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the Post Office Department recommended a new building at Cam-rose?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT

The minister has laboured a
great deal in an endeavour to explain why this item has not appealed in the estimates this year. He might just as well be frank and tell the committee that the real reason why this item was cut out was because the hon. member for Camrose did not support the government on all occasions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT

Yes, and yet I could not get any closer to the minister than my hon. friend seems to be able to get. I do not think his reasoning is very good

British Columbia-Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $40,000.

speechtext:
I regret that there is no
provision made in this vote for a public building in Trail. I regret that particularly because there seems to have gone out from the government to the people of Trail information to the effect that a vote for a public building in Trail would be "noted" in the supplementary estimates. I presume that what is meant by "noted" is considered, and I hope that such will be the case. We are not, like some of our friends from Saskatchewan and elsewhere, asking for a public building in Trail simply because we want to get a whack at the public treasury, but because in Trail there is urgent need of a public building. We have an industrial institution with a continuous pay roll, and it is not necessary for us to come down here and make inroads upon the public treasury just to get a few thousand dollars spent there. We have there a pay roll of approximately $5,000,000 a year, and I am asking for this public building solely because it is in keeping with the policy laid down by the hon. Minister of Public Works last session, when he said that the policy of the government was to construct buildings where the accommodation was inadequate and the need urgent. I think that is a very sane and sensible policy. It sounds more like a Conservative policy, and I want to congratulate the minister upon having laid it down.
The first intimation we had from the government about a public building in Trail came
2896	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
from the hon. Minister of Health, formerly the Minister of Public Works. He notified the Trail board of trade that this item would be noted by the government and of course the people of Trail were pleased to hear that. The city of Trail then sent a telegram to the minister, stating that they had received such advice, and urging the immediate construction of this building for the reason that the accommodation was inadequate and the necessity urgent. They went further and passed a resolution emphasizing this urgency. The resolution goes on to say, in keeping with the general prosperity of Trail:
Whereas the number of boxes in the post office is at present 1,047, and whereas the present requirements are 2,500-
That is a little stronger than I put it before, but evidently the city seems to think that their requirements are a little more than double the present accommodation. The resolution goes on:
Owing chiefly to the rent of the present premises having been increased from $75 to $115 a month, the postmaster in like manner has increased the rent for the boxes from 2o to 33 per cent.
There are 1,047 boxes in use in the Post Office, and there are 500 people waiting for boxes; in addition, there are from three to five families using many boxes. I am confident that the minister will admit that that is a case of inadequate accommodation.
Considerable has been said to-day about the growth of the various communities for which votes have been asked. To-day the governor general is laying the comer stone of a new city hall for Trail. That is pretty good evidence of prosperity. The people of Trail by public subscription are preparing for the erection of a $200,000 hotel. That is a little better than some of these Saskatchewan hotels. Within the last two years there have been erected a $100,000 hospital and a $45,000 artificial ice rink; and within the last two months there has been constructed a new $75,000 theatre. This large industrial company at Trail of which I spoke has loaned [DOT] to its employees $700,000 for the erection of homes. I would like to know if you can get any better evidence of prosperity and progress.
The city of Trail in the past five years has grown beyond all bounds. During that time they have carried on construction work, street paving, a water system and so forth, to the amount of $475,000, and the Canadian Pacific Railway has just completed the construction of a new brick station. I submit to the Minister of Public Works that the Can-

adian Pacific Railway is not building stations except in places where the requirements of the people demand it. Within the last five years the city of Trail has issued building permits to the value of $1,731,000. I have taken the precaution, Mr. Chairman, to get these figures from the city clerk, so there can be no dispute about them-$1,731,000 in building permits in Trail within the past five years; what better evidence could you have of progress? The company at Trail has also disbursed within the last five years $7,800,000 for construction work. When you consider all these evidences of prosperity, it is difficult to realise how any fair-minded government could hesitate to meet the requirements of the city of Trail.
In addition, the city of Trail pays into the federal exchequer in business and income taxes $1,000,000 a year-$1,000,000 a year from this little city'" of Trail, for the purpose of building wharves down in Quebec province and public buildings in Saskatchewan. Then we pay into the provincial exchequer $800,000. As a matter of fact, the city of Trail pays in taxes to the federal exchequer three times as much as this parliament votes for public buildings in the entire province of British Columbia. The city of Trail and its industrial plant pay in excess of one per cent of the total freight bill by rail and by water for the entire Dominion.
Now, what is needed is a three-storey building to take care of the postal and customs requirements. The customs collections for the past year amounted to $120,000. That is a pretty good figure for a small community. The post office revenue for 1926-27 was $20,381. Trail post office ranks nineteenth out of the 941 post offices in British Columbia. By way of rent, interest and incidental expenses in connection with the post office and the customs office the government pays the equivalent every year of 5 per cent on $90,000.
Much has been said in behalf of some other communities about their growth of population. Trail's population has increased in the last five years from $5,000 to 8,500. The government post office inspector has reported to the department that in two or three years the population will probably reach 12.000. Just compare this with the vote of $28,000 passed this afternoon for a post office at Rosthern, Saskatchewan, which has only 271 boxes, and it needs another 40. We have 1,047 boxes, and the post office inspector reports that 500 people are waiting for accommodation. The Minister of Public Works justified the Rosthern vote on the ground of lack of accommodation. Then we have the right hon.

Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) coming from Prince Albert, and Prince Albert is voted $95,000 on the plea that in twenty years its population has grown from 1,785 to 7.500. It didn't take Trail twenty years to wake up; in three years its population increased from 5,000 to 8,500. Then we have an appropriation for Waterloo, Quebec, with a population of 2,000 and a revenue of $7,804. There are several cases of that kind appearing in the estimates while Trail with its much larger population and postal revenue is ignored.
I think it is generally admitted throughout the country that it is unfair for any member or any community to ask for public improvements that are not needed, and I commend the Minister of Public Works for discouraging such applications. But surely this has been about the largest spending program of any government since confederation. We have voted $8)500,000 for Quebec harbour, $6,000,000 to beautify Ottawa, $100,000 last year and another $150,000 this year for Quebec citadel, $100,000 last year and a similar sum this year for Rideau Hall, and $30,000 for a greenhouse. I merely mention those votes by way of comparison with the small sum which is asked for a community that is actually suffering for want of adequate post office facilities.
I have a letter here which I have hesitated to read, because it is rather amusing in view of the huge sums which have been voted. It comes from the hon. Minister of Health (Mr. King), who was formerly in charge of the Department of Public Works. It is his second letter to the Trail board of trade. For some reason or other he seems to have changed his attitude, foT which I am very sorry, and I do hope that the present Minister of Public Works will not be influenced by his colleague. He says:
The Minister of Public Works informs me that it is felt by the government that it is better to continue the reduction of taxation and payments on the national debt,-

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROC EDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, it is amusing, and hard to believe in view of about twenty million dollars voted recently. Let me continue: -and this can only be done by strict economy and delaying, for the present, any undertakings which, although necessary, are not essential to the carrying on of the public business.
If that is not a joke, I do not know what is, particularly following the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, in which he noted a surplus of $54,000,000 and said that the estimated revenue for the coming year wa3 56103-184
sufficient to meet the needs of a growing country.
I have dealt with the inadequacy of the accommodation in the buildings at Trail. Now I am going to refer to the urgency for a new building. On October 6-and may I ask hon. members to recall that the genera, election came on October 29, 1925-the hon. Minister of Health, was at that time Minister of Public Works and distributing such patronage as he could on the eve of the election, purchased in Trail a site for a post office. That is, he did so three weeks before the election, and this is what I wish to impress upon the present Minister of Public Works and my friends on the other side of the house so that they may observe how the former head of the department regarded this matter. The Public Works department, of which, as I say, the present Minister of Health was then the head, sent the following wire to the surveyor:
Make the survey of these lots with the utmost despatch, as the matter is very urgent.
That was three weeks before the election. If it was so urgent back in 1925, why has it not been urgent enough since to proceed with the construction of the building? But that is not all. The then Minister of Public Works sent another letter in which he says that he is quite familiar with the necessities of the situation, and that he purchased the site with a view to the construction of a building. I am merely giving these facts to impress upon the government, if it is possible, that I am entirely within, bounds in urging the construction of this building, not because we want to get at the treasury, but simply because we need the accommodation. There are many days when the men come off shift, line up on the sidewalk waiting to get their mail, and after vainly waiting for half an hour or more they find it useless to remain longer and go home disappointed. Surely that is evidence of the necessity and urgency of better accommodation. Let me quote a letter from the post office inspector who has sent to Trail to investigate conditions. Under date of December 16, 1926, he wrote to the department:
I would respectfully request that a new building be erected as soon as possible. Three times more floor space required. There are now 1,047 boxes and 500 people are waiting.
He recommended that the new building should contain 2,100 boxes. That is evidence enough of the necessity. I present these facts in the hope that the minister from British Columbia will put aside political prejudice and follow the policy laid down by the Min-

Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
ister of Public Works, and give to a growing community of wage earners the accommodation so urgently needed.
We had another letter which I shall be pleased to read. This one comes from the Minister of Health; it is addressed to myself. He says:
I am thoroughly conversant-
You see, the Minister of Health is aware of the needs of the district. He says he is thoroughly conversant with them.
I am thoroughly conversant with the matters of that district, and it was with a view of giving better accommodation that I recommended the purchase of a property in Trail some time ago,-
He was a little reticent about saying when.
-it being my intention to advocate the erection of a suitable building on the site.
The situation just comes down to this. The Minister of Health is certainly in a peculiar position. He is a member of the cabinet and he cannot go to Trail and say, "I have not recommended your post office", because he has already intimated that the supplementary vote would be considered. It would not be healthy for him to go to Trail.

speechtext: I always find it very healthy there.

speechtext:
I may remind the Minister of Health, with all courtesy, that he was out there last autumn and was within an hour's ride of Trail; and yet, curiously enough, he passed by us and went up the lake. He could not go there and say that he had not recommended the vote. The Minister of Health is in fact in a most embarrassing position and a position of humiliation if he says to his colleagues in the cabinet, "I firmly and honestly believe that the vote is necessary and I urge you to provide in the supplementary estimates for a public building in Trail", if that representation is to be disregarded. I should not like to be in the position of a minister of a government who could not receive sufficient attention from his colleagues to meet his wants in a matter of this kind, particularly when, as in this case, the hon. gentleman is the sole cabinet representative of the province of British Columbia. I may say that all we have got in British Columbia from this government is the Minister of Health.
I am now going to conclude these remarks with a courteous request of the Minister of Public Works and the other members of the cabinet. I appeal to them not to disappoint the citizens of Trail in regard to this post office.

I have another letter here-I have saved the best for the last. This letter is dated January 4, 1927, from the Postmaster General, who naturally receives reports from all quarters. Under this date he sends me a letter in which he says:
I have already made representations to the department (Public Works) that the accommodation at present provided at Trail is totally inadequate-
The Postmaster General says that the accommodation provided at Trail is totally inadequate, and it is on that basis that I trust the Minister of Public Works will meet our wishes in this matter. He continues:
*-and have urged-
He has not asked them, mind you; he has urged:
the erection of a suitable public building.
My appeal to the minister and to the government will, I hope, be entertained. I know we are on the wrong side of the fence, but it was not altogether our fault.

speechtext: We pretty nearly got you in Trail.

speechtext: Never mind about Trail. The Minister of Health should not say anything at all in regard to votes. He managed to slip into his seat by a slim 275 votes, and if he is well advised he will slip into the senate at the first opportunity that offers.

speechtext:
I feel sure the post office for Trail will appear in the supplementary estimates. I wish to congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Esling) on the case he has put up and I am sure the minister and the cabinet cannot very well turn down the Trail post office. There is one matter I want to refer to. Anyone who will casually glance over the estimates for public buildings in the province of British Columbia will be struck by this fact, that, outside the city of Vancouver, the amount for new buildings is jusit $29,000. It is quite apparent that British Columbia has been overlooked. We do not know whether it is because we are so far from the capital-some 3,000 miles distant- or whether it is because of the political complexion of the province. At any rate there is some reason for it. It seems to me that the Trail post office and applications for other public buildings in that province should be considered in the supplementary estimates. As I say, the amount for buildings in British Columbia, outside Vancouver, is $29,000, although we find in'the votes the other day the sum of $30,000 allotted to cleaning up a site west of the post office in the city of

Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
Ottawa-$1,000 more than the sum given to the province of British Columbia for public buildings outside of Vancouver. Then we find, coming to Saskatchewan, in Prince Albert, with a population of 7,500 a vote of $95,000 for public buildings this year, making a total of $133,000 for public buildings in the district of Prince Albert.
The minister has said that it is the intention to provide accommodation, in certain towns and cities, sufficient to facilitate the carrying on of the various services. The other day we had a number of items for public buildings, in connection with which the postal revenue ranged from $2,000 u,p to $6,900, and I find that in the Fraser valley district it is twenty years since we have received a vote for any public building. I have here an application which was made to the government by the Mission City Board of Trade some time ago, directing attention to the fact that a lot had been purchased a number of years ago, in 1911 or 1912 I think, an amount having been voted for the construction of a building. That amount was subsequently revoted, but it disappeared, because of the conditions which existed during the war. Now the government apparently have undertaken to commence a program of construction throughout the Dominion, and certainly the people of these cities and towns in this district expected to receive consideration.
Mission City is the centre of one of our greatest fruit districts; the Minister of Health will bear me out when I say that it is one of the centres of the small fruit district of the Fraser valley, and has developed considerably in the last few years. The post office in that town is housed in a very small frame structure. The postal revenue is given by the Post Office department as $6,669.21, and in addition a rural route is served. A lot has been purchased, and as I have already said appropriations have been voted and revoted; the people of that district feel that they have waited patiently and that they are entitled to some consideration now that the government have commenced to provide buildings in such centres. Many other places with smaller revenues are receiving grants; I might mention the town of Wainwright, which has a postal revenue of about $5,000, and for which we have voted an amount tonight to provide for a public building. I would ask that the government and the minister consider the case of Mission City and see if something cannot be done.

Then there is the town of Abbotsford, which is one of the customs ports of entry. We all know that the customs commission recommended that many inland ports be closed, but it is certain that a port such as Abbotsford must be retained. The Board of Trade of that town took up this matter on July 19 in regard to accommodation for the post office and for the Customs department; they pointed out that three railways meet at that point, namely, the Canadian PacificRailway, the Great Northern Railway and the British Columbia Electric Railway, and the revenue from customs imports and exports and the postal revenue has greatly increased during recent years. I belieye the board of trade have already communicated with the minister in regard to this matter. Last year the customs revenue amounted to about $75,000 and the postal revenue to over $4,000, making a total of almost $80,000. It will be easy to realize the conditions which exist with regard to the Customs department when you consider that they pay only $185 a year for their accommodation, 'although the revenue amounts to about $75,000. This is a port which will remain; it is just on the border, and is in the centre of a rapidly growing district. This town should receive attention in the very near future, and I would ask the minister to take these facts into consideration. I must say the people in British Columbia are disappointed with the very small vote for public buildings in that province and we hope the government will consider the applications which have been made for public buildings and provide for them in the supplementary estimates.

As the government has
renewed the lease on the Prince Rupert post office for five years, I suppose we cannot ask for a new post office, but I would like to point out the condition of our Dominion public building in Prince Rupert.
I would like to draw the attention of the committee to a few points, and I can illustrate what I am going to say by reference to the Prince Rupert post office. On February 13 I asked certain questions of the Postmaster General. Some of the questions I asked him were:
What is the annual rental paid by the government for its lease of said building?
When does the present lease expire?
Has the lease recently been renewed, and if so, on what date?
The answers were as follows: It was leased for five years; rented on June 1, 1927, to terminate June 1, 1932, at a rental of $6,540.
I also asked who recommended the renewal of the lease, and the answer given was:
The various departments interested.
I endeavoured to find out who were the parties interested. I found that it was not the citizens of Prince Rupert as a body; it was not the board of trade representing the city of Prince Rupert, but it was confined to a very small section, and that section, undoubtedly, does not hold the views of the people of the city. I will leave it to the hon. members of this committee to know who recommended the renewal of that lease. _
I wish to read a letter from the Prince Rupert board of trade, asking this government to do something towards meeting the requirements of that city. The letter is as follows: That as the building now' leased at Prince Rupert for federal offices, such as customs, post office, government telegraphs, marine and fisheries, harbour master, excise department, Indian agent, etc., is hopelessly lacking in accommodation and is badly arranged, poorly ventilated and altogether unsuited for the occupancy of the Dominion government offices in this city; and as the rentals paid for these offices are sufficient to justify and provide for the erection of a suitable federal building upon the government's own property situate in a more central and convenient location: therefore, that representation should be made to the
Dominion government, urging the immediate erection of a federal building ir. Prince Rupert, in keeping with the requirements of the city, and that the lease of the building now used be not renewed, except for such period as may be necessary for the completion of the new building.
I am now going back to the hon. Minister of Public Works, and will refer to his own statement, given in answer to one of the hon. members from the prairie provinces, as to why Saskatoon was given a vote of $150,000. The answer was not satisfactory to me, because it was not based, I thought, upon sound reason. Here is what the minister said.
The reason why this vote was given to Saskatoon was on account of the increased trade and revenue.
And then, later on:
Twenty years ago the revenue was $19,711, and in 1927 it was $280,943.

It was originally a gymnasium for the young men belonging to a local society. It never was and never has

been intended for a public building. Furthermore it is unhygienic; secondly, it is hopelessly inadequate for the large amount of work that is carried on therein, and, thirdly, it is not in the centre of the city. It was placed in its present position-and I am sorry to say this in the house where men are supposed to be above common politics-for the good not of the city but of the member at that time. It is completely out of the way, on a side street; it is not meeting the requirements of the city trade and it is so hopelessly inadequate for the amount of work that is being carried on that last Christmas the postmaster issued a public notice begging the people to come to his aid in order to enable him and his staff to cope with the heavy amount of work. The condition of affairs last Christmas can be described as confusion and chaos. Christmas letters and Christmas parcels could not be delivered as they should. The staff was not to blame. Mail to the outlying islands did not reach their destination; in the hurry, excitement and hubbub where hundreds of thousands of letters were going into that wretched place, mail to the islands was often sent to wrong places. This information I had from people who have written to me.
I wish to say just this, because I believe it is for the good of all. These Dominion buildings are as important as parliament buildings, the reason being that in these federal buildings we carry on our customs and excise and other important business. They stand as the external proof of law and order and in our cities where federal work is being carried on, the buildings should teach the people that in them things are being conducted in a law abiding manner, meetihg every requirement of public life. Surely a filthy, unsightly, wretched building is by no means in keeping with the work which a federal government should carry on. Second, the principles under which our Dominion buildings should be erected should not be actuated by political exigencies. They should be based on a sound and definite principle. Are they really needful? What requirements are to be met? If necessity be the basis on which public buildings should be erected and if the minister here to-night is able to tell us that Saskatoon is entitled to $150,000, merely because of a slight increase in its revenue, then I say that as intelligent people we have good reason to object to certain of these votes.
Therefore I say on behalf of the people of British Columbia and, indeed, every other province of Canada that the hour has come when any government in power should place

its public works department completely out of the control of politics; there should be nothing of politics in it. Why should a former member of parliament be the final judge whether this or that building should be erected? Why should I have to come here and plead for something w'hich it should be the duty of the Minister of Public Works to know is required? He has the machinery; he has his federal engineers in his own department to give him the facts. We waste endless time in connection with these matters and we get nowhere. I know what I say now will not get me a post office because there is a five-year lease in existence; but even if there were no five-year lease I do not believe my words would enable me to succeed in getting what I want. Nevertheless I know as well as I stand here that if the Minister of Public Works, the Prime Minister or any other member of the cabinet went and looked at that building, he would admit that it is unfit, not merely for carrying on federal work but for any man or woman to spend six or eight long hours therein.
For fifteen years I was presiding examiner for the Civil Service Commission. It was my duty to supervise the examinations and I shall never forget the comic-tragedy of the examination papers sent out by the Civil Service Commission for applicants for positions of janitors in the post office. I am sorry I have not a copy of these papers under my hand but I can get one. These unfortunate people, whose hours were spent in nothing more than a stable, with poor ventilation, with doors that would not open properly on their hinges, with a roof that could be blown off by an ordinary wind, were asked questions such as these. What method would you adopt in order to ventilate a post office? What are the various hygienic things that are essential for the cleansing and keeping in proper order of a Post office building? I sat down myself while three of those unfortunates were scratching their heads, wondering, and I said to myself: If these men get five per cent out of a hundred they are better men than I am. I am afraid they did not get that five per cent. I have just a simple question to ask. Are we to continue carrying along on the same old lines of tit for tat? Is it because in the past something was done, we shall do the same? Or is it possible, when we come to the important question of deciding how the money of this country shall be spent on public works, that they shall be spent where the money is needed, where it will do the most good and bring the greatest return?
